articles.title: A brain cell atlas integrating single-cell transcriptomes across human brain regions
articles.evidence: Peer-reviewed research; integrated single-cell transcriptomic datasets
articles.summary: Researchers assembled a reference atlas of human brain cells using single-cell gene-expression studies from multiple brain regions. The atlas describes cell-type diversity and regional variation; it is not an exhaustive map of every individual brain.
articles.question: Why is a multi-region, multi-donor brain atlas more informative than studying one brain region?
articles.answer: It helps capture both regional and individual biological variability instead of assuming one sample represents the entire brain.

articles.title: Single-cell multiregion dissection of Alzheimer’s disease
articles.evidence: Peer-reviewed, open access; post-mortem multiregion single-cell study
articles.summary: This study compared cells from several brain regions in donors with and without Alzheimer’s disease. It describes vulnerable cell populations and possible signaling mechanisms, without establishing a clinical diagnostic test.
articles.question: Why should a brain disease study sample several regions instead of relying on one area?
articles.answer: Disease-related changes may vary by region and cell type, so one area can miss important differences.

articles.title: The golden ratio—dispelling the myth
articles.evidence: Published critical review; not a validation of mystical geometry
articles.summary: The author evaluates popular claims linking golden-ratio proportions to human facial beauty and finds no convincing evidence for using those claims as clinical design rules. Ratios may still be measured and tested with reproducible methods.
articles.question: Does finding a ratio near 1.618 prove that the golden ratio controls biological form?
articles.answer: No. Researchers need reproducible landmarks, comparisons with alternative models, and statistical evidence beyond a numerical resemblance.

articles.title: Human genetic variations conferring resistance to malaria
articles.evidence: Published review; geographic genetic variant frequencies must not be treated as racial essences
articles.summary: The review discusses how malaria exposure shaped the distribution of several genetic variants across populations. Environmental histories and specific variants matter more than broad racial labels.
articles.question: Why is sickle-cell trait not accurately described as belonging to one race?
articles.answer: Its distribution tracks malaria-related evolutionary history across multiple geographic populations; broad race categories are not a genetic diagnosis.
